keyVerseText: Though he be fruitful among his brethren, an east wind shall come, the wind of the LORD shall come up from the wilderness, and his spring shall become dry, and his fountain shall be dried up: he shall spoil the treasure of all pleasant vessels. pleasant: Heb. vessels of desire
rootMeaning: The Hebrew verb פָּרָא (pârâʼ) is a primitive root that fundamentally means "to be fruitful" or "to bear fruit." While no further etymological detail is provided, its core sense revolves around the natural process of producing fruit, which implies growth, productivity, and life. This literal root sense enriches the common English gloss by emphasizing not just the act of fruitfulness but the inherent vitality and generative power behind it.
usageInScripture: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, translated as "Though he be fruitful" in Hosea 13:15. The singular occurrence and consistent translation highlight its clear and focused meaning related to fruitfulness or productivity. The use in this context underscores both literal and metaphorical fruitfulness among brethren, pointing to a broader spiritual or communal vitality that can be present even amidst impending judgment.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding פָּרָא as "to be fruitful" is vital for grasping biblical themes of blessing, covenantal promise, and spiritual growth. Fruitfulness in Scripture often symbolizes God’s blessing and the outworking of His life-giving power in His people. From a Christ-centered perspective, this word points toward the spiritual fruitfulness that believers are called to bear through the Holy Spirit. Recognizing the root meaning reminds Christians that true fruitfulness is not merely external success but the manifestation of God’s life within, which ultimately leads to eternal blessing and reflects the character of Christ.
keyVerseReflection: Hosea 13:15 states, "Though he be fruitful among his brethren, an east wind shall come... and his spring shall become dry." Here, פָּרָא conveys a paradox: fruitfulness exists, yet it is overshadowed by coming judgment. The word highlights a temporary or superficial productivity that will be cut off by God’s sovereign intervention. This deepens the verse’s warning that external fruitfulness without faithfulness or dependence on God is ultimately futile, reminding believers to seek enduring fruitfulness that flows from God’s blessing.
